title: Molybdenum chain

chokepoint.physics: About half a by-product of copper mining (the rest primary); diversified across Chile/China/US/Peru — coupled, but not a severe chokepoint

eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · the metal that takes the heat
h1: The metal that lets steel take the heat — and mostly a copper by-product
deck: Molybdenum is a quiet alloying workhorse: a small addition makes steel stronger, harder and able to hold its strength at high temperature, which is why it is in stainless steel, tool steel and the superalloys of turbines and reactors. It also catalyses the removal of sulfur from fuels. About half of it comes as a by-product of copper mining.
byline: copper by-product (~half) + primary mines ≠ ferro-molybdenum / oxide ≠ high-strength & superalloy steel · desulfurisation catalysts
correction: Molybdenum is essential but not a severe chokepoint — a useful contrast to its neighbours. Roughly half of it is recovered as a by-product of copper mining and the rest from primary mines, spread across Chile, China, the United States and Peru, so no single country controls it. Its importance is functional: it hardens and heat-proofs steel (superalloys, stainless, tool steel) and it makes the hydro-desulfurisation catalysts that strip sulfur out of diesel and jet fuel, tying it to the sulfur chain.

panels.h3: A little goes a long way
panels.text: Adding a few percent of molybdenum to steel raises its strength, hardness, weldability and corrosion and heat resistance. It is what lets stainless steel resist pitting, tool steel hold an edge, and pipeline and pressure-vessel steel take stress. In nickel-based superalloys it helps jet-engine and power-turbine parts survive extreme heat — a small, essential input across heavy industry.

Molybdenum-based catalysts drive hydro-desulfurisation — the refinery process that removes sulfur from diesel, petrol and jet fuel to meet clean-air rules. So the same metal both strengthens the steel of the refinery and enables the chemistry inside it, and its catalyst demand links directly to the sulfur chain.

sections.h2: 2 · Coupled to copper, but spread out

panels.text: About half of world molybdenum is a by-product of large copper mines (its molybdenite occurs alongside copper sulfides), and the other half comes from primary molybdenum mines such as Climax and Henderson in Colorado and operations in China. Because it is both a by-product and a primary product, and mined across several countries, its supply is more elastic and less concentrated than a pure by-product like tellurium or rhenium.

Molybdenum has not been weaponised or cornered: supply is diversified, recycling from steel scrap is significant, and price rather than availability is the usual concern. It sits in the atlas as the case of an essential alloying metal that is genuinely well-supplied — a reminder that 'critical to industry' and 'a supply chokepoint' are not the same thing.
